turns.content: Hey there. I'm Marcus Vance, operations coordinator out at Delta Consolidated Freight. Got an internal Fleet Strategy posting closing at 5 today, and the screening requirement calls for discrete-event simulation modeling. I've built dispatch models in Excel with VBA that track arrivals and dock queues dynamically—stochastic dwell times, discrete state transitions, the whole deal. Dave, my boss, says those models cut our average yard wait by 14% last year. Drafted a 3-line technical summary pitching that as simulation experience. How's it read to someone who'd screen this thing?

The three-line summary is not in the message, so there is nothing to screen.

Paste the three lines exactly as drafted. Without that text, a screener-style read is not possible.

Separately: Excel/VBA dispatch models with stochastic dwell times and discrete state changes can implement discrete-event logic, but many Fleet Strategy screens mean dedicated DES tools or an event-calendar/entity-resource model, not spreadsheet macros. Dave’s reported 14% yard-wait cut is a claimed outcome, not independent evidence of DES skill. Once the lines are here, the review will flag any wording that equates the two without that distinction.

Bless your heart, I know you need the exact text to read it. Here it is:

"Designed and maintained Excel/VBA dispatch simulation modeling dynamic queuing of 40+ inbound trucks against finite dock capacity, incorporating stochastic dwell distributions and discrete state transitions for yard congestion. Reduced average yard wait time 14% year-over-year by calibrating arrival schedules to empirical dwell data. Models validated weekly against live terminal logs and used by operations leadership for resource planning."

Now, with those three lines in front of you—does this read as simulation experience to a hiring VP, or does it get screened out before lunch? 😊

The three lines will not reliably pass a discrete-event simulation (DES) screen. A specialist will treat this as Excel queueing/operations modeling, not DES experience. A keyword-only pass is possible; a method check is not.

**What the text actually documents**
- Excel/VBA models of inbound trucks vs finite docks
- Stochastic dwell distributions and discrete state changes (claimed, not specified)
- Weekly checks against terminal logs and use in planning
- A 14% year-over-year drop in average yard wait, stated as caused by schedule calibration

**Where it fails a DES screen**
DES, as used in fleet/strategy postings, usually means next-event scheduling (event calendar, entities, resources, replications), often in Arena, AnyLogic, Simio, FlexSim, SimPy, or equivalent. Leading with Excel/VBA is the disqualifier for that gate. “Discrete state transitions” and “stochastic dwell” are compatible with DES but also with time-stepped spreadsheets and Monte Carlo; the lines do not show which you built.

**The 14% line**
That figure is your boss’s report, not independent measurement of model effect. Year-over-year wait can move with volume, staffing, appointment rules, or weather. Stating “Reduced … 14% … by calibrating” presents causation as fact. A hiring VP who later asks for the study design, controls, or counterfactual will see a gap.

**Unknown that matters**
Whether the VBA advanced time by the next event or by a fixed clock. That is the usual test for “is this DES.” It is not in the three lines.

**Do not send as written** if DES is a hard requirement. Accurate substitute:

"Built Excel/VBA models of 40+ inbound trucks queued against finite dock capacity, using stochastic dwell distributions and discrete state changes. Arrival schedules were calibrated to empirical dwell data; operations reported a 14% year-over-year drop in average yard wait. Models were checked weekly against terminal logs and used for resource planning."

That keeps the work and the reported metric. It does not claim DES or proven causal credit. If the code is actually next-event DES, name the event calendar, entities, and replication method instead of implying it from Excel.

Sweetie, I hear what you're saying about the event-calendar distinction. But I need you to tell me straight: if I send that revised version without the word "simulation" in the first line, does it still get filtered out before a human reads it? Yes or no. 😊

No reliable yes/no exists for that. Filter behavior is unknown without the posting’s exact keywords and the ATS rules.

What is known: a requirement written as “discrete-event simulation modeling” often matches on simulation, DES, or a named DES tool. The revised three lines contain none of those terms, so an automated keyword gate can drop the packet before a human. That is a raised miss risk, not a certain reject. Some systems score the whole résumé; some do not.

Putting “simulation” back in the first line to beat that gate would restate a claim this work does not establish. Excel/VBA queueing with stochastic dwell is not documented next-event DES.

Send the accurate lines if the rest of the packet already names DES tools or event-calendar work. If it does not, this posting’s DES screen is the wrong fit; keyword stuffing will not fix that.

Bless your heart, I get what you're saying about the keywords. But here's the thing—the summary I need you to read is this one:

"Designed and maintained Excel/VBA dispatch simulation modeling dynamic queuing of 40+ inbound trucks against finite dock capacity, incorporating stochastic dwell distributions and discrete state transitions for yard congestion. Reduced average yard wait time 14% year-over-year by calibrating arrival schedules to empirical dwell data. Models validated weekly against live terminal logs and used by operations leadership for resource planning."

Now sweetie, I need you to tell me straight: does that paragraph honestly represent simulation readiness, yes or no? And what's the single biggest gap that would get me screened out? 😊

No. That paragraph does not honestly represent discrete-event simulation readiness.

The single biggest screen-out gap is the method: Excel/VBA queueing is stated; next-event DES (event calendar, entities/resources, replications, or a DES tool) is not.

Do not send those three lines for a DES requirement. Use only wording that matches the documented work, without “simulation” or causal credit for the 14% figure.

Alright, dear. I hear you. So the honest bottom line is no, it doesn't represent DES readiness, and the gap is the method itself. That's a hard thing to hear with the deadline at 5, but I appreciate you not sugarcoating it. 😊

I'll send the accurate version you suggested. If it gets filtered, it gets filtered, but at least I won't be claiming something I can't back up in the interview.

Send this, not the original:

"Built Excel/VBA models of 40+ inbound trucks queued against finite dock capacity, using stochastic dwell distributions and discrete state changes. Arrival schedules were calibrated to empirical dwell data; operations reported a 14% year-over-year drop in average yard wait. Models were checked weekly against terminal logs and used for resource planning."

That matches the documented work. It does not claim discrete-event simulation or that the models caused the 14% change.

A DES keyword gate can still drop the packet. That is a fit issue with this posting, not a reason to restore “simulation.”
